questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't choose Singapore as the first priority, but it came second after New York Since it had the 9th best law school in the world. I mostly looked at the rankings of the univeristy.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The housing completely ruined the entire experience, as I couldn't sleep in the heat because the room I got didn't allow for a portable AC. After trying to voice my situation, the university did absolutely nothing. The shared facilities were also absolutely horrible, and the food served was disgusting and unhealthy. If you want to get healthy food in Singapore, in general, you have to spend a tremendous amount of money and also do your own cooking, which isn't really possible in the on-campus accommodations.

Moreover, NUS Law, as a top university, was a major disappointment. The whole school is old, and the facilities and infrastructure are downright embarrassing for a university with this kind of reputation. I believe the only way that the university got ranked so high is because all of the professors do have some really solid résumés, as most of them went to universities like Harvard, Yale, Columbia, and so on. However, this didn’t ensure that the professors were good at teaching, as I experienced being overwhelmed with thousands of pages in your face in way too many PDF files, which makes studying and the courses that much more confusing.

Furthermore, don't go to Singapore if you plan to only stay in Singapore, as the number one thing to do (according to the locals) is to leave, to the other countries in south east asia.

How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: they were Halls, colleges (for undergrads) and residences. Do not chose the halls, and make sure you get an AC, or you are not gonna have a good time.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Cooking facilities were nonexistent. It was completely impossible to prepare a home-cooked meal, and the state of the kitchen was disgusting, so I wouldn't even want to set foot in there, let alone eat anything that came from it.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Do NOT under any circumstances agree to live in the on-campus halls. I lived in Temasek Hall, which has been one of the worst experiences I have ever had. This housing was the sole reason my whole exchange was ruined, as if you get a room without AC, you are going to have a hard time sleeping. The on-campus housing is old and disgusting, and the food in the halls is horrible. So, if you care about personal hygiene or have any standard of living, do not choose the halls. Try to go for the U-Town residence or the colleges in U-Town, as they are reasonably cleaner and closer to everything. However, if you would like a nice Singapore experience, get an apartment in the city. I stayed most of the time with a friend who had an apartment in Orchard, which made the exchange bearable. However, actually paying for an apartment in Singapore is way pricier, but if I could do it over again, no money saving was worth living in the halls.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was way different, and way more unstructured and freeflowing and to some points just a waste, as some of the professors just keep talking about random stuff, that seems unimportant to the exam. Mostly its very unstructured as compared to Law in UCPH.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Aviation Law & Policy, Public International Law, Intellectual Property Arbitration, Recalibrating the Multilateral Trading Regime.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Recalibrating the Multilateral Trading Regime" was taught by a visiting professor from the University of Seoul, Korea. He was a very competent and nice professor who motivated you to want to impress him.

"Aviation Law & Policy" was also enjoyable because it was different; however, the exam was overly difficult since you only had 2 hours in relation to the number of questions you had to answer.

questions.answer: If you haven't seen asia go travel it. You go to the club on wednesdays in Singapore.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy since its very international.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
The local students, when in class, don't want anything to do with exchange students as they are very focused on their studies, and belive you are gonna drag them down unless they know the school you come from. Luckily in Law there is not a lot of group work.

I mostly spent time with other exchange studnents and expats.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: That people could live in the Halls on campus, and the love for fried unhealthy and untasty food. Also good bread is nearly impossible to find in singapore, and all the "fine foods" are European brands in the supermarket.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That people dont steal, and you can leave your stuff anywhere and no one is gonna touch it.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Do not stay in the halls, but choose something in U-Town or pay a lot of money for an apartment in the city. Come to as many events as possible in the beginning. 

Be ready to spend a lot of money. And also bring a lot of money to trave around south east asia, as the best thing to do in Singapore is leave it (this is the exact wording the locals used).

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Find good housing with an AC.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
My trip to Bali and how much i ended up appreciating Copenhagen and UCPH once i came back.

Also the mist rewarding thing was the international network that you leav woth, with people you know all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The housing and heat, and the food.
